# 1. The story

Almost all of the CO₂ humans have put into the air came from a small number
of countries, over a short stretch of time, and the warming it causes
tracks that running total closely. This document tells that story in three steps:

1. **Analysis (Part 2).** A standard tidyverse pipeline (import, inspect,
   tidy, transform, visualise, model) asks four questions of the data. How
   fast have emissions grown? What were they made of? Who emitted them? How
   unequal are emissions per person today? And how closely does warming
   follow the cumulative total?
2. **Artwork for the eye (Part 3).** *The Human Smokestack* is a streamgraph
   that pours out of a factory chimney and widens as the world industrialises.
   Each band is a region and each band ends in its own totals.
3. **Artwork for the ear (Part 4).** *Breath of the Chimney* is a 26-second
   sonification of 1850–2025. The smoke is noise that grows louder, the three
   largest emitters are a chord, and the warming is a drone that rises in
   pitch.

Part 5 uses the two artworks to answer the assignment's two questions.

# 2. Analysis: the data science pipeline

## 2.1 Import

The data is Our World in Data's CO₂ and Greenhouse Gas Emissions dataset
(<https://github.com/owid/co2-data>). This document reads the copy of
`owid-co2-data.csv` saved next to it. If that file is missing, it reads the
latest version from GitHub instead.

```{r import}
csv_path <- if (file.exists("owid-co2-data.csv")) "owid-co2-data.csv" else
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/owid/co2-data/master/owid-co2-data.csv"
co2 <- read_csv(csv_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

dim(co2)            # rows x columns
range(co2$year)     # time span covered
```

## 2.2 Inspect

Each row is one country or region in one year, with
`r ncol(co2)` columns. The columns used in this document are:

```{r inspect}
co2 %>%
  select(country, year, iso_code, population, co2, coal_co2, oil_co2,
         gas_co2, cement_co2, flaring_co2, other_industry_co2,
         cumulative_co2, cumulative_co2_including_luc,
         temperature_change_from_co2) %>%
  glimpse()

# how complete is the World series for each column we rely on?
co2 %>%
  filter(country == "World") %>%
  summarise(across(c(co2, coal_co2, oil_co2, gas_co2, cement_co2, flaring_co2,
                     cumulative_co2_including_luc, temperature_change_from_co2),
                   ~ paste(range(year[!is.na(.x)]), collapse = "–"))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "years with data") %>%
  kable()
```

All emissions are in **million tonnes of CO₂ (Mt)**. The `co2` column counts
fossil fuels and industry only. Land-use change, such as deforestation, is
counted separately.

## 2.3 Tidy

The file mixes real countries with aggregates such as "World", "Africa",
"European Union (27)" and income groups. Adding them together would double
count. Countries have a three-letter ISO code. Aggregates have either no
code or an `OWID_` code, so the two can be separated cleanly.

```{r tidy}
countries <- co2 %>%
  filter(!is.na(iso_code), !str_starts(iso_code, "OWID"))
world <- co2 %>% filter(country == "World")
last_year <- max(world$year[!is.na(world$co2)])

n_distinct(countries$country)   # number of countries
last_year

# the six fossil/industrial sources, from wide columns to one long column
source_cols <- c(Coal = "coal_co2", Oil = "oil_co2", Gas = "gas_co2",
                 Cement = "cement_co2", Flaring = "flaring_co2",
                 Other = "other_industry_co2")
world_sources <- world %>%
  select(year, co2, all_of(source_cols)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-c(year, co2), names_to = "source", values_to = "mt") %>%
  # a missing source before it existed (oil before 1855, flaring before
  # 1950, ...) means no emissions from it, so 0
  mutate(mt = replace_na(mt, 0),
         source = factor(source, levels = names(source_cols)))

# sanity check: the six sources add up to the total in every year
world_sources %>%
  group_by(year, co2) %>%
  summarise(sum_sources = sum(mt), .groups = "drop") %>%
  summarise(largest_gap_mt = max(abs(sum_sources - co2)))
```

The six sources add up to the total to within a rounding error in every
year, so the long table is safe to stack.

## 2.4 How fast did emissions grow, and from what?

```{r sources-plot, fig.cap="World CO₂ emissions from fossil fuels and industry by source, 1750–2025"}
source_colors <- c(Coal = "#3b3b3b", Oil = "#8c5a2b", Gas = "#4a7fb0",
                   Cement = "#b8b2a6", Flaring = "#e07b39", Other = "#9a7fb8")

ggplot(world_sources, aes(year, mt / 1000, fill = source)) +
  geom_area(color = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = source_colors, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1750, 2025, by = 25), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = " bn t"), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "World CO₂ emissions by source",
       subtitle = "Billion tonnes per year, fossil fuels and industry") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "top")
```

```{r source-shares}
first_last <- world_sources %>%
  filter(year %in% c(1900, 1950, last_year)) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  mutate(share = mt / sum(mt)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(year, source, share) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = share)
first_last %>% mutate(across(-source, percent_format(accuracy = 0.1))) %>% kable()
```

Coal was almost the whole story until 1900. Oil and gas only became major
sources after 1950, and coal is still the largest single source in
`r last_year`.

To measure growth, a model of the form `log(co2) ~ year` is fitted to each
historical period. The slope of that line is the average yearly growth
rate, and `log(2) / slope` is the doubling time.

```{r growth}
periods <- tribble(
  ~period,                  ~from, ~to,
  "Industrial take-off",     1850, 1913,
  "Wars and depression",     1914, 1945,
  "Post-war boom",           1946, 1973,
  "Oil shocks to 2000",      1974, 2000,
  "21st century",            2001, last_year
)

growth <- periods %>%
  mutate(fit = map2(from, to, ~ lm(log(co2) ~ year,
                                   data = filter(world, year >= .x, year <= .y))),
         tidied = map(fit, ~ tidy(.x, conf.int = TRUE) %>% filter(term == "year")),
         r2 = map_dbl(fit, ~ glance(.x)$r.squared)) %>%
  unnest(tidied) %>%
  transmute(period, years = paste0(from, "–", to),
            growth = exp(estimate) - 1,
            ci_low = exp(conf.low) - 1, ci_high = exp(conf.high) - 1,
            doubling_years = log(2) / estimate, r2)

growth %>%
  mutate(across(c(growth, ci_low, ci_high), percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)),
         doubling_years = round(doubling_years),
         r2 = round(r2, 3)) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Period", "Years", "Growth / yr", "95% CI low",
                      "95% CI high", "Doubling time (yrs)", "R²"))
```

```{r growth-values, include=FALSE}
growth_of   <- function(p) growth$growth[growth$period == p]
doubling_of <- function(p) round(growth$doubling_years[growth$period == p])
```

There were two bursts of very fast growth. From 1850 to 1913 emissions grew
about `r percent(growth_of("Industrial take-off"), 0.1)` a year, doubling every
`r doubling_of("Industrial take-off")` years, and the post-war boom matched it at
`r percent(growth_of("Post-war boom"), 0.1)`. Since the 1970s growth has slowed to
about `r percent(growth_of("21st century"), 0.1)` a year. That is slower growth, but
not a decline: on top of today's base it still adds hundreds of millions of
tonnes every year.

The confidence intervals assume each year is independent of the next.
Emissions series are strongly autocorrelated, so the true uncertainty is
wider than shown. The point estimates are the part to rely on.

## 2.5 Who emitted it?

```{r top10, fig.height=5, fig.cap="The ten countries with the largest cumulative CO₂ emissions, 1750–2025"}
top10 <- countries %>%
  filter(year == last_year) %>%
  slice_max(cumulative_co2, n = 10) %>%
  mutate(country = fct_reorder(country, cumulative_co2))

top10_share <- sum(top10$share_global_cumulative_co2) / 100

ggplot(top10, aes(cumulative_co2 / 1000, country)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#6b4a2f", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(share_global_cumulative_co2, 1), "%")),
            hjust = -0.15, size = 3.8, color = "#2b2b2b") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = " bn t"),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = paste0("Cumulative CO₂ emissions, 1750–", last_year),
       subtitle = "Labels show each country's share of the world's cumulative total") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

Ten of the `r n_distinct(countries$country)` countries account for
`r percent(top10_share, 1)` of all fossil CO₂ emitted since 1750. The United
States alone accounts for
`r percent(top10$share_global_cumulative_co2[top10$country == "United States"] / 100, 0.1)`.

## 2.6 How unequal is it today?

A Lorenz curve answers this question. It ranks countries from lowest to
highest emissions per person, then plots each group's share of the world's
population against its share of the world's emissions. The further the curve
sags below the diagonal, the more unequal emissions are. The Gini
coefficient summarises the sag in one number: 0 means everyone emits the
same, and 1 means one person emits everything.

```{r lorenz, fig.width=7, fig.height=6.5, fig.cap="Lorenz curve of national per-person CO₂ emissions"}
ineq <- countries %>%
  filter(year == last_year, !is.na(co2), !is.na(population), population > 0) %>%
  mutate(per_capita = co2 / population) %>%
  arrange(per_capita) %>%
  mutate(pop_share = cumsum(population) / sum(population),
         em_share  = cumsum(co2) / sum(co2))

lorenz <- bind_rows(tibble(pop_share = 0, em_share = 0),
                    select(ineq, pop_share, em_share))
gini <- 1 - sum(diff(lorenz$pop_share) *
                (head(lorenz$em_share, -1) + tail(lorenz$em_share, -1)))
bottom50 <- approx(lorenz$pop_share, lorenz$em_share, xout = 0.5)$y
top10pop <- 1 - approx(lorenz$pop_share, lorenz$em_share, xout = 0.9)$y

ggplot(lorenz, aes(pop_share, em_share)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "22", color = "#9a968e") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, color = "#9c1f4a") +
  annotate("point", x = 0.5, y = bottom50, size = 3, color = "#9c1f4a") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.52, y = bottom50 - 0.03, hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 4,
           label = paste0("The lowest-emitting half of humanity\nemits ",
                          percent(bottom50, 1), " of the CO₂")) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.55, y = 0.62, angle = 45, size = 3.6, color = "#9a968e",
           label = "perfect equality") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent, expand = c(0, 0.01)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, expand = c(0, 0.01)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Share of world population (lowest per-person emitters first)",
       y = "Share of world CO₂ emissions",
       title = paste0("Who emits, ", last_year),
       subtitle = paste0(nrow(ineq), " countries · Gini = ", round(gini, 2))) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

In `r last_year`, the countries that hold the lowest-emitting half of the
world's population emitted only `r percent(bottom50, 1)` of the CO₂. The
highest-emitting tenth emitted `r percent(top10pop, 1)`. This calculation
treats every person in a country as emitting that country's average. It
cannot see inequality between people within the same country, so the true
inequality between individuals is higher than this Gini of `r round(gini, 2)`
suggests.

## 2.7 From emissions to warming

If the human contribution drives warming, warming should follow the
cumulative total of CO₂ emitted, not each year's emissions. This chunk
regresses the dataset's estimate of global warming caused by CO₂ on the
world's cumulative CO₂, including land-use change, for every year from 1851
to 2024.

```{r warming, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.5, fig.cap="Estimated warming from CO₂ against cumulative CO₂ emitted, 1851–2024"}
warm <- world %>%
  filter(!is.na(temperature_change_from_co2), !is.na(cumulative_co2_including_luc)) %>%
  mutate(cum_gt = cumulative_co2_including_luc / 1000)   # billion tonnes

warm_fit <- lm(temperature_change_from_co2 ~ cum_gt, data = warm)
tidy(warm_fit, conf.int = TRUE) %>% kable(digits = 6)
glance(warm_fit) %>% select(r.squared, sigma, nobs) %>% kable(digits = 5)

per_1000 <- coef(warm_fit)[["cum_gt"]] * 1000   # °C per 1,000 billion tonnes

ggplot(warm, aes(cum_gt, temperature_change_from_co2, color = year)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#2b2b2b", linewidth = 0.6,
              linetype = "22") +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "inferno", end = 0.9, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(big.mark = ",", suffix = " bn t")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = " °C")) +
  annotate("text", x = 300, y = 1.05, hjust = 0, size = 4.2,
           label = paste0("≈ ", round(per_1000, 2), " °C of warming\nper 1,000 billion tonnes emitted")) +
  labs(x = "Cumulative CO₂ emitted since 1850 (including land-use change)",
       y = "Global warming caused by CO₂",
       title = "Warming tracks the running total of emissions") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

The relationship is almost perfectly straight (R² =
`r round(glance(warm_fit)$r.squared, 4)`). Each 1,000 billion tonnes of CO₂
adds about **`r round(per_1000, 2)` °C** of warming. This matches the IPCC's
best estimate of about 0.45 °C per 1,000 billion tonnes, its "transient
climate response to cumulative emissions". By `r max(warm$year)` humans had
emitted `r comma(round(max(warm$cum_gt)))` billion tonnes, which by this
relationship accounts for about `r round(max(warm$temperature_change_from_co2), 2)` °C
of warming.

The near-perfect R² needs care. OWID did not measure this temperature
column with thermometers. It estimated it from emissions with a simple
climate model, so a strong fit is partly built in. What the regression
shows is that the dataset is internally consistent with established climate
science. It does not prove that relationship independently. Observed warming
also includes effects from methane, nitrous oxide and aerosols.

# 3. Artwork for the eye: *The Human Smokestack*

The first artwork turns sections 2.4 to 2.6 into a single image. A
streamgraph pours out of a factory chimney in 1950 and keeps widening to `r last_year`.
Each band is a region. Its thickness in any year is that
region's emissions, and its numbers at the right edge are its `r last_year`
emissions and its total since 1950. The chimney's smoke runs straight into
the bands. The metaphor is that every band is smoke from the same stack, and
the stack is human industry.

The sections below build the artwork step by step.

### 3.1 The time span and the series

The artwork reuses the `co2` table imported in Part 2. It starts in 1950,
when every region has a recorded value in every year, and runs to the last
year in the file.

```{r art-series}
# the full range of the dataset: first to last year with a World figure
Y0 <- 1950   # chart start (the dataset itself starts in 1750)
Y1 <- max(co2$year[co2$country == "World" & !is.na(co2$co2)])

# when each series used below starts and ends in the file
sources <- c("United Kingdom", "European Union (27)", "United States", "China",
             "India", "Russia", "Japan", "Canada", "Africa", "South America",
             "Asia", "World")
coverage <- co2 %>%
  filter(country %in% sources, !is.na(co2)) %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(first = min(year), last = max(year), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(first)
coverage

# one country/region's annual CO2 (Mt) for every year Y0..Y1.
# Before a series' first recorded year it has no recorded emissions, so 0;
# the occasional missing year inside a series is filled in linearly
# from the years either side.
get_series <- function(name) {
  d <- co2 %>% filter(country == name, year >= Y0, year <= Y1, !is.na(co2))
  v <- approx(d$year, d$co2, xout = Y0:Y1, rule = 1)$y
  v[Y0:Y1 < min(d$year)] <- 0
  v
}
```

### 3.2 Building the twelve categories

The chart follows the same regional breakdown a lot of "CO2 through time"
explainers use: seven individual countries (the UK included, since it is the whole story
before 1800), the EU-27 as a bloc, two continental
aggregates, and two remainder categories so everything still sums to the real
world total in every single year.

```{r categories}
china  <- get_series("China")
us     <- get_series("United States")
india  <- get_series("India")
russia <- get_series("Russia")
japan  <- get_series("Japan")
canada <- get_series("Canada")
uk     <- get_series("United Kingdom")
eu     <- get_series("European Union (27)")   # OWID's own current-members aggregate
africa <- get_series("Africa")                 # OWID continent aggregate
sam    <- get_series("South America")          # OWID continent aggregate
asia   <- get_series("Asia")                   # OWID continent aggregate
world_v <- get_series("World")

# Asia minus the three Asian countries already broken out on their own
asia_excl <- asia - china - india - japan

# whatever is left once every named category is subtracted from the world
# total (Oceania, non-EU Europe, the rest of the Americas, etc.)
named_sum <- china + us + india + russia + japan + canada + uk + eu + africa + sam + asia_excl
rest_of_world <- world_v - named_sum

# OWID's aggregates and country series come from slightly different sources
# in the earliest years, so the remainder can dip a hair below zero there.
# Check it is negligible, then clip it.
stopifnot(min(rest_of_world) > -0.02 * max(world_v))
rest_of_world <- pmax(rest_of_world, 0)

years <- Y0:Y1

# stacking order, bottom -> top
order <- c("China", "Asia (excl. China, India, Japan)", "United States",
           "European Union", "United Kingdom", "Rest of World", "India", "Russia",
           "Africa", "South America", "Japan", "Canada")

mat <- rbind(china, asia_excl, us, eu, uk, rest_of_world, india, russia, africa,
             sam, japan, canada)
rownames(mat) <- order
n <- nrow(mat); m <- ncol(mat)
```

### 3.3 A wiggle-free "silhouette" streamgraph baseline

A streamgraph is a stacked area chart whose baseline floats instead of
sitting at zero, so the whole stack reads as a symmetric, organically
expanding band rather than a wall rising off the x-axis. The classic
ThemeRiver construction centers the stack at every year:

```{r baseline}
totals <- colSums(mat)
baseline <- -totals / 2   # symmetric baseline: top = +total/2, bottom = -total/2

ymin_mat <- matrix(0, n, m)
ymax_mat <- matrix(0, n, m)
cum <- baseline
for (i in seq_len(n)) {
  ymin_mat[i, ] <- cum
  cum <- cum + mat[i, ]
  ymax_mat[i, ] <- cum
}
rownames(ymin_mat) <- order
rownames(ymax_mat) <- order

long <- lapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
  tibble(year = years, category = order[i],
         ymin = ymin_mat[i, ], ymax = ymax_mat[i, ], thickness = mat[i, ])
}) %>%
  bind_rows() %>%
  mutate(category = factor(category, levels = order))
```

### 3.4 Colors, and automatic label contrast

Each band keeps one fixed color. Rather than hand-pick a text color per
label, we compute the [relative luminance](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG20/#relativeluminancedef)
of each band's color and choose black or cream text automatically — this is
what lets every country name sit *directly inside* its own colored band
cleanly, instead of needing a separate legend.

```{r colors}
colors <- c(
  "China" = "#9c1f4a", "Asia (excl. China, India, Japan)" = "#d98c82",
  "United States" = "#1a6fa3", "European Union" = "#f2c230",
  "United Kingdom" = "#6b4a2f",
  "Rest of World" = "#a6a6a6", "India" = "#e2863a", "Russia" = "#2437d6",
  "Africa" = "#1f6b3a", "South America" = "#8a3b8f", "Japan" = "#f3b8c4",
  "Canada" = "#2f9e8f"
)

text_color_for <- function(hex) {
  rgb <- col2rgb(hex) / 255
  lin <- ifelse(rgb <= 0.03928, rgb / 12.92, ((rgb + 0.055) / 1.055)^2.4)
  L <- 0.2126 * lin[1] + 0.7152 * lin[2] + 0.0722 * lin[3]
  if (L > 0.45) "#1a1a1a" else "#f5f1e6"
}
label_colors <- setNames(vapply(colors, text_color_for, character(1)), names(colors))

# A few band colors (pale pink, pale sand) work fine as fills but read poorly
# as *text* against the cream page background. Darken just the text variant
# for those — the ribbon, connector lines, and legend dots keep the true color.
darken_label <- function(hex, amt = 0.35) {
  rgb <- col2rgb(hex) / 255
  if (mean(rgb) > 0.62) rgb <- rgb * (1 - amt)
  rgb(rgb[1], rgb[2], rgb[3])
}
text_colors <- setNames(vapply(colors, darken_label, character(1)), names(colors))
```

### 3.5 Placing the labels: inside the band, or above it

The names are set in one straight column near the right end of the stream
(see the next section), each centered in its own band, the way the reference
infographic does it. The helpers below are kept for the label search used
elsewhere in the document.

```{r label-placement}
thin_categories <- c("Canada", "Japan", "South America")

window_df <- long %>% filter(year >= 1995, year <= Y1 - 7)
best <- window_df %>%
  group_by(category) %>%
  slice_max(thickness, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(mid = (ymin + ymax) / 2,
         is_thin = category %in% thin_categories,
         label = ifelse(category == "Asia (excl. China, India, Japan)",
                         "Asia (excl. China,\nIndia, Japan)", as.character(category)))

max_total <- max(totals)
BG <- "#f5f1e6"  # warm off-white background, matches the reference infographic

direct <- best %>% filter(!is_thin)

pointer <- best %>%
  filter(is_thin) %>%
  mutate(year = c(Canada = 2019, Japan = 2011, `South America` = 1998)[as.character(category)]) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(mid = {
    i <- which(order == as.character(category))
    j <- which(years == year)
    (ymin_mat[i, j] + ymax_mat[i, j]) / 2
  }) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(label_y = max_total * 0.60)
```

### 3.6 Each band's numbers, attached to the end of the band

Rather than a separate table that repeats every name, each region's numbers
are written right where its band ends in `r Y1`, in the band's own color,
set right against the band's end. The color and the position are the link. Both figures come straight out of
`mat`: the last column for the `r Y1` value, `rowSums(mat)` for the
`r Y0`–`r Y1` total, in billions of tonnes.

```{r band-numbers}
# Same y-envelope the plot uses (coord_cartesian below)
ylim_lo <- -max_total * 0.66
ylim_hi <- max_total * 0.74
axis_y  <- ylim_lo + max_total * 0.015
axis_ticks <- seq(Y0, Y1, by = 10)

latest_val <- setNames(mat[, m] / 1000, order)      # billions of t, in Y1
cum_val    <- setNames(rowSums(mat) / 1000, order)  # billions of t, Y0-Y1

end_df <- tibble(
  category = factor(order, levels = order),           # China (bottom) ... Canada (top)
  target   = (ymin_mat[, m] + ymax_mat[, m]) / 2,     # middle of each band in Y1
  v1       = latest_val[order],
  v2       = cum_val[order],
  col      = unname(colors[order]),
  txt      = unname(text_colors[order])
)

# Each row sits level with its own band. Where thin bands are too close for
# two lines of text, push rows upward just enough to clear each other; the
# connector still starts at the band's true position.
min_gap <- max_total * 0.021
y <- end_df$target
for (i in 2:length(y)) y[i] <- max(y[i], y[i - 1] + min_gap)
end_df$y <- y

num_v1 <- Y1 + 0.6     # this year's value, right against the band's end
num_v2 <- Y1 + 5.0    # cumulative value
div_x  <- Y1 + 4.4    # thin divider between the two columns
head_y <- max(end_df$y) + min_gap * 2.2
x_max  <- Y1 + 10

# Names: one straight column, centered at name_x, each at the middle of its
# own band in that year. Bands thick enough get the name inside (smaller type
# for the thin ones); a band too thin for any text gets it just above.
name_x <- 2014       # a flat stretch before the 2020 dip
win <- which(years >= name_x - 4 & years <= name_x + 4)   # years the name text spans
name_df <- tibble(
  category = factor(order, levels = order),
  label    = recode(order, "Asia (excl. China, India, Japan)" = "Asia\n(excl. China,\nIndia, Japan)",
                    "Rest of World" = "Rest of\nWorld", "European Union" = "European\nUnion",
                    "United Kingdom" = "U.K.",
                    "United States" = "U.S."),
  # average middle of the band across those years, so the name sits squarely
  # in its own band even where the band slopes or dips (2020)
  y        = rowMeans((ymin_mat[, win] + ymax_mat[, win]) / 2),
  ymax     = apply(ymax_mat[, win], 1, max),
  thick    = apply(mat[, win], 1, min),
  col      = unname(colors[order]),
  txt      = unname(text_colors[order])
) %>%
  mutate(inside = thick >= 800 & !category %in% c("South America", "United Kingdom"),
         fs     = case_when(category == "Asia (excl. China, India, Japan)" ~ 3.9, thick >= 4000 ~ 4.6, thick >= 2500 ~ 4.0, thick >= 1300 ~ 3.0, TRUE ~ 2.7))

# South America's name is too long for its thin band, and the U.K.'s band is
# too thin for any text, so both get a pointer: the name above the stream and
# a thin line down into the band
make_pointer <- function(cat, yr, lab) {
  i <- which(order == cat); j <- which(years == yr)
  tibble(x = yr, label = lab,
         y_mid = (ymin_mat[i, j] + ymax_mat[i, j]) / 2,
         y_lab = totals[j] / 2 + max_total * 0.085,
         col = colors[[cat]], txt = text_colors[[cat]])
}
sa_pointer <- bind_rows(make_pointer("South America", 1984, "South America"),
                        make_pointer("United Kingdom", 2001, "United Kingdom"))
```

### 3.7 The three call-out facts (kept entirely off the colors)

These sit in the blank cream background to either side of the thin early
stream (1950s) — never on top of a colored band — with a thin leader line
running from the text down (or up) to the data point it describes.

```{r annotations}
env_top <- function(yr) totals[years == yr] / 2
env_bot <- function(yr) -totals[years == yr] / 2

# Every number in the three call-outs is computed here from the data.
total_over <- function(name, yrs) sum(co2$co2[co2$country == name & co2$year %in% yrs], na.rm = TRUE)

# 1. the 1950s, and everything emitted before 1950 (1750-1949)
fifties  <- 1950:1959
before50 <- 1750:1949
us_50s     <- total_over("United States", fifties) / total_over("World", fifties)
europe_50s <- (total_over("European Union (27)", fifties) + total_over("United Kingdom", fifties)) /
  total_over("World", fifties)
west_pre50 <- (total_over("United States", before50) + total_over("European Union (27)", before50) +
  total_over("United Kingdom", before50)) / total_over("World", before50)

# 2. China, 1950 -> 1980
china_1950   <- china[years == 1950]
china_1980   <- china[years == 1980]
china_growth <- round((china_1980 / china_1950 - 1) * 100)
china_fold   <- round(china_1980 / china_1950)

# 3. today: the three largest emitting countries, and the rest of Asia as a group
top3_share <- (china[years == Y1] + us[years == Y1] + india[years == Y1]) / world_v[years == Y1]
asia_share <- asia_excl[years == Y1] / world_v[years == Y1]

# check that China, the U.S. and India really are the three largest countries
countries_now <- co2 %>% filter(year == Y1, !is.na(iso_code), !str_starts(iso_code, "OWID"))
stopifnot(identical(sort(slice_max(countries_now, co2, n = 3)$country),
                    sort(c("China", "United States", "India"))))

# a bracket under the text spanning the 1950s, with an arrow from it down
# into the middle of the U.S. band in 1955
us_mid_1955 <- long %>% filter(category == "United States", year == 1955) %>%
  mutate(mid = (ymin + ymax) / 2) %>% pull(mid)
ann1 <- list(x = 1952, y = 12200,
             bracket_x = c(1950, 1959), bracket_y = 9000,
             arrow_x = 1955, arrow_yend = us_mid_1955,
             label = sprintf(paste0("In the 1950s, the U.S. and Europe (EU-27 + U.K.)\n",
                                    "emitted %s of the world's CO\u2082."),
                             percent(us_50s + europe_50s, 1)))

ann2 <- list(x = 1952, y = -13600, xstart = 1961, ystart = -12900,
             xend = 1969, yend = env_bot(1969) * 1.03,
             label = sprintf(paste0("Between 1950 and 1980, China's yearly emissions grew\n",
                                    "%s-fold (+%s%%), from %s to %s billion tonnes."),
                             china_fold, format(china_growth, big.mark = ""),
                             round(china_1950 / 1000, 2), round(china_1980 / 1000, 1)))

ann3 <- list(x = 1952, y = -18600,
             label = sprintf(paste0("Today, three countries (China, the U.S. and India)\n",
                                    "emit %s of the world's CO\u2082. The rest of Asia,\n",
                                    "taken together, emits another %s."),
                             percent(top3_share, 1), percent(asia_share, 1)))

# 4. the line under the title: what came before the chart starts
pre_years   <- min(co2$year[co2$country == "World" & !is.na(co2$co2)]):(Y0 - 1)
all_years   <- min(pre_years):Y1
pre_total   <- total_over("World", pre_years)
pre_share   <- pre_total / total_over("World", all_years)
pre_groups  <- c(
  "the U.S."      = total_over("United States", pre_years),
  "the EU-27"     = total_over("European Union (27)", pre_years),
  "the U.K."      = total_over("United Kingdom", pre_years),
  "Russia"        = total_over("Russia", pre_years),
  "China"         = total_over("China", pre_years),
  "India"         = total_over("India", pre_years),
  "Japan"         = total_over("Japan", pre_years),
  "Canada"        = total_over("Canada", pre_years),
  "Africa"        = total_over("Africa", pre_years),
  "South America" = total_over("South America", pre_years),
  "the rest of Asia" = total_over("Asia", pre_years) - total_over("China", pre_years) -
                       total_over("India", pre_years) - total_over("Japan", pre_years)
) / pre_total
pre_top <- sort(pre_groups, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]          # the three largest groups
pre_top_txt <- paste0(names(pre_top), " (", percent(pre_top, 1), ")")
intro_line <- sprintf(paste0("The record begins in %d. By %d the world had already emitted %s billion tonnes, ",
                             "%s of everything emitted to date,\nmostly by %s, %s and %s."),
                      min(pre_years), Y0, comma(round(pre_total / 1000)), percent(pre_share, 1),
                      pre_top_txt[1], pre_top_txt[2], pre_top_txt[3])
intro_line

flags <- tibble(lab = c("CN", "US", "IN"),
                 col = c(colors[["China"]], colors[["United States"]], colors[["India"]]),
                 x = c(1952, 1954.3, 1956.6))
```

### 3.8 The smokestack the stream comes out of

The chimney photo (`chimney.png`, saved next to this file) stands at the left
edge, with its smoke running straight into the start of the stream in `r Y0`.
The photo is placed so its plume sits level with the stream's start,
its base sits on the time axis, and it keeps its own proportions. The stream
is drawn on top, so the colored bands come out of the smoke.

```{r smokestack}
chimney_img <- png::readPNG("chimney.png")
img_ratio <- dim(chimney_img)[1] / dim(chimney_img)[2]   # height / width in pixels

smoke_frac <- 0.18          # the plume's middle, as a share of the photo's height from the top
stack_H    <- -axis_y / (1 - smoke_frac)                    # photo height in data units
stack_ymax <- smoke_frac * stack_H
stack_ymin <- axis_y

# convert the photo's height into a width in years, using the panel's size
# in inches, so it isn't stretched
panel_w_in <- 17.0; panel_h_in <- 8.6
x_range <- (x_max - (Y0 - 7.5)); y_range <- ylim_hi - ylim_lo
stack_h_in <- stack_H / y_range * panel_h_in
stack_w    <- (stack_h_in / img_ratio) / panel_w_in * x_range
stack_xmax <- Y0 + 1.0       # smoke tucks just under the stream's first year
stack_xmin <- stack_xmax - stack_w

smoke_end <- Y0 + 2          # (used to drop band outlines inside the smoke)
```

### 3.9 The plot

```{r plot, fig.width=17.5, fig.height=10.2, fig.cap="CO2 emissions through time, by region, 1950-2025, each band labeled with its own totals (Our World in Data)"}
ggplot(long, aes(x = year, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax, fill = category)) +
  # chimney photo, drawn first so the stream sits on top of its smoke
  annotation_raster(chimney_img, xmin = stack_xmin, xmax = stack_xmax,
                    ymin = stack_ymin, ymax = stack_ymax, interpolate = TRUE) +
  # the stream: the same thin cream separators between bands in every year
  geom_ribbon(color = BG, linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colors, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +

  # one straight column of names near the right end, each inside its band
  geom_text(data = filter(name_df, inside),
            aes(x = name_x, y = y, label = label, color = category, size = fs),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, family = "sans", fontface = "bold", lineheight = 0.88) +
  scale_color_manual(values = label_colors, guide = "none") +
  scale_size_identity() +
  # the one band too thin to hold its name (Canada) gets it just above its top edge
  geom_segment(data = sa_pointer, aes(x = x, xend = x, y = y_mid, yend = y_lab - max_total * 0.008),
               inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.6, color = sa_pointer$col) +
  geom_text(data = sa_pointer, aes(x = x, y = y_lab, label = label),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, fontface = "bold", size = 4.0, vjust = 0, color = sa_pointer$txt) +
  geom_text(data = filter(name_df, category == "Canada"),
            aes(x = name_x, y = ymax + max_total * 0.008, label = label),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, fontface = "bold", size = 3.4, vjust = 0,
            color = filter(name_df, category == "Canada")$txt) +

  # call-out annotations, entirely in the cream background
  annotate("segment", x = ann1$bracket_x[1], xend = ann1$bracket_x[2],
           y = ann1$bracket_y, yend = ann1$bracket_y, linewidth = 0.5, color = "#2b2b2b") +
  annotate("segment", x = ann1$bracket_x, xend = ann1$bracket_x,
           y = ann1$bracket_y - max_total * 0.008, yend = ann1$bracket_y + max_total * 0.008,
           linewidth = 0.5, color = "#2b2b2b") +
  annotate("segment", x = ann1$arrow_x, xend = ann1$arrow_x,
           y = ann1$bracket_y, yend = ann1$arrow_yend, linewidth = 0.5, color = "#2b2b2b",
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.12, "inches"), type = "open")) +
  annotate("text", x = ann1$x, y = ann1$y, label = ann1$label, hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
           size = 4.3, family = "sans", color = "#2b2b2b", lineheight = 1.25) +
  annotate("segment", x = ann2$xstart, y = ann2$ystart, xend = ann2$xend, yend = ann2$yend,
           linewidth = 0.5, color = "#2b2b2b") +
  annotate("text", x = ann2$x, y = ann2$y, label = ann2$label, hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
           size = 4.3, family = "sans", color = "#2b2b2b", lineheight = 1.25) +
  annotate("text", x = ann3$x, y = ann3$y, label = ann3$label, hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
           size = 4.3, family = "sans", color = "#2b2b2b", lineheight = 1.25) +
  geom_point(data = flags, aes(x = x, y = -17500), inherit.aes = FALSE, shape = 16,
             size = 9, color = flags$col) +
  geom_text(data = flags, aes(x = x, y = -17500, label = lab), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            size = 2.6, fontface = "bold", color = "white") +

  # bottom axis, drawn by hand so it can sit below the floating baseline
  annotate("segment", x = Y0, xend = Y1, y = axis_y, yend = axis_y, linewidth = 0.6,
           color = "#2b2b2b") +
  annotate("text", x = axis_ticks, y = axis_y - max_total * 0.018,
           label = axis_ticks, size = 4.2, vjust = 1, color = "#2b2b2b", family = "sans") +

  # numbers set right against the end of each band, in the band's color
  geom_text(data = end_df, aes(x = num_v1, y = y, label = number(v1, accuracy = 0.1)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = 0, fontface = "bold", size = 3.4, color = end_df$txt) +
  geom_text(data = end_df, aes(x = num_v2, y = y, label = number(v2, accuracy = 0.1)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = 0, fontface = "bold", size = 3.4, color = end_df$txt) +
  annotate("segment", x = div_x, xend = div_x, y = head_y - min_gap * 0.45,
           yend = min(end_df$y) - min_gap * 0.6, linewidth = 0.3, color = "#cfc8b8") +
  annotate("text", x = num_v1, y = head_y + min_gap * 1.15,
           label = "Tonnes of CO\u2082\nin billions", hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 3.2,
           color = "#8a8a8a", lineheight = 0.95, family = "sans") +
  annotate("text", x = num_v1, y = head_y, label = as.character(Y1), hjust = 0,
           size = 3.2, color = "#8a8a8a", family = "sans") +
  annotate("text", x = num_v2, y = head_y, label = paste0(Y0, "\u2013", Y1), hjust = 0,
           size = 3.2, color = "#8a8a8a", family = "sans") +

  # the line under the title about the years before 1950
  annotate("text", x = Y0 - 7.3, y = ylim_hi + max_total * 0.055, label = intro_line, hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
           size = 4.6, family = "serif", color = "#3a3a3a", lineheight = 1.15) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off", xlim = c(Y0 - 7.5, x_max), ylim = c(ylim_lo, ylim_hi)) +
  labs(title = "CO₂ Emissions Through Time",
       subtitle = paste0(Y0, "–", Y1)) +
  theme_void(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.background  = element_rect(fill = BG, color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = BG, color = NA),
    plot.margin      = margin(16, 18, 10, 18),
    plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 30, hjust = 0, family = "serif",
                                  margin = margin(b = 2)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(face = "bold", size = 18, hjust = 0, family = "serif",
                                  margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.caption  = element_blank()
  )
```

### 3.10 Reading the chart

- **Shape**: the stack is centered (a "silhouette" streamgraph), so both the
  top and bottom edges swell outward over time — the visual read is "the
  world's carbon footprint widening," not just a line going up.
- **Labels**: every name sits in one straight vertical column near the
  right end, inside its own band, with text color chosen by contrast. The
  position is averaged over a few flat years before the 2020 dip so each
  name stays inside its band. Canada is too thin to hold text, so its name
  sits just above its band.
- **Call-outs**: the three framing sentences, and their leader lines, are
  positioned only in the blank cream background — never on top of a band —
  by finding each year's actual top/bottom envelope and placing the text
  safely outside it.
- **Time range**: `r Y0`–`r Y1`. The dataset starts in 1750; this chart
  shows `r Y0` onward, and every region has recorded data for every year in
  that range. The right-hand totals cover `r Y0`–`r Y1`.
- **Call-out numbers**: every figure in the three call-outs is computed in
  section 3.7, not typed in. The first covers the 1950s; the years before
  1950 are covered by the line under the title. The third names China, the U.S. and India as the
  three largest single countries (the code checks this), and gives the rest
  of Asia's share separately. As a group of countries, the rest of Asia
  emits more than the U.S.
- **The numbers**: every band ends in `r Y1` with its own figures beside it,
  in its own color — the `r Y1` total and the `r Y0`–`r Y1` running total, in
  billions of tonnes. There is no separate table repeating the names: the
  figures sit right against the end of each band, and the thinnest bands'
  figures are nudged apart just enough to stay legible. Both numbers are read
  out of `mat`, the same matrix that draws the stream, so the two can never
  disagree.

# 4. Artwork for the ear: *Breath of the Chimney*

A chart shows the whole period at once, so a reader can see that emissions
rose without feeling how quickly. Sound plays out in time, so a listener
experiences it as it happens. *Breath of the Chimney* compresses 1850–`r last_year`
into about half a minute. Each year lasts 0.15 seconds. Four layers carry
the data:

```{r sound-mapping, echo=FALSE}
tribble(
  ~Layer,             ~`What you hear`,                                   ~`Data it carries`,
  "Smoke",            "filtered noise, like a roaring chimney or wind",     "world CO₂ each year → loudness",
  "Three voices",     "an A-major chord (A3, C♯4, E4)",                      "U.S., EU-27 and China CO₂ → loudness of each note",
  "Warming drone",    "a low hum that slowly rises in pitch",                "warming from CO₂ → pitch (one octave per 0.5 °C)",
  "Clock",            "a soft tick",                                         "the start of every decade"
) %>% kable()
```

The noise suits emissions because CO₂ is invisible and shapeless: it reads
as a roar rather than a note. Each emitter's note follows its own history.
The U.S. note (A3) swells early, the EU-27 note (C♯4) swells and then fades,
and the China note (E4) is silent until the 1950s before overpowering the
others. The pitch of the drone is never reset, because warming accumulates
the same way cumulative emissions do.

## 4.1 Build the score

The score is a table with one row per year. Each column is a layer
expressed as a share of the loudest year, from 0 to 1.

```{r sound-score}
son_years <- 1850:last_year

# a country's yearly series on son_years. Years before its first record
# count as 0; the warming series stops at 2024, so its last value is held.
yearly <- function(name, var = "co2") {
  d <- co2 %>% filter(country == name, !is.na(.data[[var]]))
  v <- approx(d$year, d[[var]], xout = son_years, rule = 2)$y
  v[son_years < min(d$year)] <- 0
  v
}

score <- tibble(
  year  = son_years,
  world = yearly("World"),
  us    = yearly("United States"),
  eu    = yearly("European Union (27)"),
  china = yearly("China"),
  temp  = yearly("World", "temperature_change_from_co2")
)
peak <- max(score$world)

score %>%
  filter(year %in% c(1850, 1900, 1950, 2000, last_year)) %>%
  mutate(across(c(world, us, eu, china), ~ round(.x / peak, 3)),
         temp = round(temp, 2)) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Year", "Smoke loudness", "U.S. note", "EU-27 note",
                      "China note", "Warming (°C)"))
```

```{r sound-score-plot, fig.height=6.5, fig.cap="The score: what each layer of the sound does over time"}
score_long <- bind_rows(
  score %>% transmute(year, layer = "1. Smoke loudness (world CO₂)", voice = "World", value = world / peak),
  score %>% transmute(year, layer = "2. Chord voices (loudness)", voice = "U.S. (A3)", value = us / peak),
  score %>% transmute(year, layer = "2. Chord voices (loudness)", voice = "EU-27 (C♯4)", value = eu / peak),
  score %>% transmute(year, layer = "2. Chord voices (loudness)", voice = "China (E4)", value = china / peak),
  score %>% transmute(year, layer = "3. Drone pitch (Hz)", voice = "Warming", value = 110 * 2^(temp / 0.5))
)
voice_colors <- c("World" = "#6e6e6e", "U.S. (A3)" = colors[["United States"]],
                  "EU-27 (C♯4)" = "#c79a00", "China (E4)" = colors[["China"]],
                  "Warming" = "#2b2b2b")

ggplot(score_long, aes(year, value, color = voice)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ layer, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = voice_colors, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1850, 2025, by = 25)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "top",
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0))
```

## 4.2 Synthesise the sound

The sound is built sample by sample in base R. A tone is a sine wave, the
smoke is smoothed random noise, and each layer's loudness follows the score
smoothly from one year to the next. The result is saved as a standard
16-bit WAV file, `co2_breath.wav`, with no audio packages required.

```{r sound-synth}
sr <- 22050                     # samples per second
sec_per_year <- 0.15
n <- round(length(son_years) * sec_per_year * sr)
t_sec <- (0:(n - 1)) / sr
yr <- son_years[1] + t_sec / sec_per_year           # the year at each sample
at <- function(v) approx(score$year, v, xout = yr, rule = 2)$y

# 1. smoke: smoothed noise, loudness = world emissions
set.seed(1)
noise <- as.numeric(stats::filter(rnorm(n), rep(1 / 12, 12), circular = TRUE))
smoke <- 0.30 * at(score$world / peak) * noise / sd(noise)

# 2. the chord: one note per emitter, loudness = its emissions
tone <- function(freq, amp) amp * sin(2 * pi * freq * t_sec)
voices <- tone(220.00, 0.30 * at(score$us    / peak)) +
          tone(277.18, 0.30 * at(score$eu    / peak)) +
          tone(329.63, 0.30 * at(score$china / peak))

# 3. the drone: pitch rises one octave per 0.5 °C of CO₂-driven warming
f_drone <- 110 * 2^(at(score$temp) / 0.5)
drone <- 0.05 * sin(2 * pi * cumsum(f_drone) / sr)

# 4. the clock: a short tick at every decade
tick <- numeric(n)
for (dec in son_years[son_years %% 10 == 0]) {
  i0 <- round((dec - son_years[1]) * sec_per_year * sr) + 1
  k <- 0:round(0.03 * sr)
  idx <- i0 + k
  keep <- idx <= n
  tick[idx[keep]] <- tick[idx[keep]] +
    0.25 * exp(-k[keep] / (0.006 * sr)) * sin(2 * pi * 1500 * k[keep] / sr)
}

mix <- smoke + voices + drone + tick
mix <- mix * pmin(1, t_sec / 0.5, (max(t_sec) - t_sec) / 1.0)   # fade in / out
mix <- 0.9 * mix / max(abs(mix))

write_wav <- function(x, path, sr) {
  pcm <- as.integer(round(x * 32767))
  nbytes <- length(pcm) * 2
  con <- file(path, "wb"); on.exit(close(con))
  writeChar("RIFF", con, eos = NULL); writeBin(as.integer(36 + nbytes), con, size = 4, endian = "little")
  writeChar("WAVEfmt ", con, eos = NULL); writeBin(16L, con, size = 4, endian = "little")
  writeBin(c(1L, 1L), con, size = 2, endian = "little")                 # PCM, mono
  writeBin(c(as.integer(sr), as.integer(sr * 2)), con, size = 4, endian = "little")
  writeBin(c(2L, 16L), con, size = 2, endian = "little")                # block align, bits
  writeChar("data", con, eos = NULL); writeBin(as.integer(nbytes), con, size = 4, endian = "little")
  writeBin(pcm, con, size = 2, endian = "little")
}
write_wav(mix, "co2_breath.wav", sr)

# how loud is each part of the piece? (root-mean-square level per 25 years)
tibble(year = floor(yr / 25) * 25, x = mix) %>%
  group_by(from = year) %>%
  summarise(loudness_rms = round(sqrt(mean(x^2)), 3)) %>%
  kable()
```

## 4.3 Listen

```{r sound-player, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
cat(sprintf('<audio controls style="width:100%%" src="data:audio/wav;base64,%s"></audio>',
            base64enc::base64encode("co2_breath.wav")))
cat(sprintf("\n\n*%.0f seconds. The decade ticks mark time: one tick every 1.5 seconds.*\n",
            length(mix) / sr))
```

What to listen for:

- **1850–1945:** a quiet hiss, with the U.S. and EU-27 notes slowly coming through. The
  first doubling took `r doubling_of("Industrial take-off")` years, but from a small base, so it is easy to
  miss.
- **1946–1973:** the post-war boom. The hiss swells quickly and the U.S. and
  EU-27 notes ring together.
- **1980s onward:** the EU-27 note fades, and the China note grows until it
  is louder than both others (from the mid-2000s). By the end, the roar has drowned out the ticks.
- **The whole piece:** the drone rises slowly and never comes back down.
  Warming is the one layer that does not drop when emissions do, because it
  follows the running total.

# 5. Reflection

## 5.1 Can data art reveal patterns that conventional visualisation cannot?

Partly. Neither artwork shows a fact that the analysis in Part 2 does not
also contain: the growth rates, the shares and the warming slope are all in
the tables. But both artworks make some patterns much harder to miss.

- **Composition and growth at once.** In the line chart in section 2.4,
  total size and composition compete for attention. The streamgraph's
  centred layout shows both together: the stream widens as emissions grow,
  and the bands inside it reorder as the U.S. and EU give way to China and
  the rest of Asia.
- **Timing.** The sonification makes the listener live through the
  timeline. A chart shows a hockey-stick curve all at once. Sound makes the
  listener wait through a century of near silence, then fills the last ten
  seconds with roar. That makes the point of section 2.4 felt rather than
  read: in absolute terms, most emissions are recent.
- **Things that move together or apart.** In the chord, the listener hears
  the EU-27 note fade while the China note rises. A chart shows the same
  crossover, but in sound it is heard as one voice taking over from another.
  The rising drone also makes plain that warming does not drop back when
  yearly emissions dip, as they did in 2020.

The cost is precision. Nobody can hear "15.5 years" or read 296.3 billion
tonnes off the width of a band. That is why the streamgraph writes its
numbers at the end of each band, and why this document keeps the regression
tables next to the artworks. Data art is a way into the data, not a
replacement for analysing it.

## 5.2 Is emotional understanding a legitimate form of understanding data?

Yes, with conditions. Understanding includes knowing what matters and why,
not only knowing the numbers. Someone who can recite that the lowest-emitting
half of humanity emits `r percent(bottom50, 1)` of the CO₂, but has never
felt that this is unequal, has not fully understood the number.
Climate change is a problem about scale, accumulation and fairness. Those
are exactly the things that numbers alone tend to flatten and that artwork
can bring back.

Emotional understanding is only legitimate if the feeling is earned
honestly, and these artworks follow four rules to make sure it is:

1. **The emotion has to come from the data.** Every visual and sonic choice
   is computed from the CSV. The width of the stream, the loudness of the
   roar and the pitch of the drone are all data, not decoration.
2. **The encodings must not exaggerate.** Loudness and band width are both
   proportional to emissions, with no exaggerated scales and no cherry-picked
   start years. The early decades are quiet because they really were
   smaller.
3. **The limits must be stated.** Sections 2.4, 2.6 and 2.7 explain the
   autocorrelation in the growth model, the per-country averaging behind the
   Gini, and the fact that the warming series comes from a model.
4. **The art should lead back to the analysis.** The artwork makes people
   care, and the statistics let them check. A feeling that cannot be traced
   back to the numbers is manipulation, not understanding.

Used this way, data art does not replace analysis. It helps the findings
reach people who would never read a regression table.

# 6. Summary of findings

- World fossil CO₂ emissions rose from
  `r round(world$co2[world$year == 1850])` million tonnes in 1850 to
  `r comma(round(world$co2[world$year == last_year]))` million tonnes in `r last_year`.
  Growth peaked twice: about
  `r percent(growth_of("Industrial take-off"), 0.1)` a year in 1850–1913 and
  `r percent(growth_of("Post-war boom"), 0.1)` a year in 1946–1973.
- Ten countries account for `r percent(top10_share, 1)` of cumulative
  emissions since 1750.
- In `r last_year` the lowest-emitting half of the world's population emitted
  `r percent(bottom50, 1)` of the CO₂. The Gini coefficient across countries
  is `r round(gini, 2)`.
- In this dataset, warming from CO₂ rises by about `r round(per_1000, 2)` °C
  per 1,000 billion tonnes emitted, in line with the IPCC's estimate.

**Data and files.** The analysis uses Our World in Data, *CO₂ and Greenhouse
Gas Emissions* (<https://github.com/owid/co2-data>), from the
`owid-co2-data.csv` in this folder. To knit this document, keep
`owid-co2-data.csv` and `chimney.png` in the same folder as the `.Rmd`.
Knitting writes `co2_breath.wav` to that folder.
